Clinical Reference · Hepatology

Acute Liver Failure

On this page
Rapid loss of liver function — coagulopathy (INR ≥ 1.5) plus any degree of hepatic encephalopathy — in a patient without pre-existing cirrhosis, evolving over < 26 weeks. A multi-organ emergency: the two things that kill are cerebral edema and sepsis/multi-organ failure, and the clock to a transplant center starts now.
INR ≥ 1.5 + HE, no cirrhosis Acetaminophen ≈ 45% of US cases Overall ~30% die / need transplant N-acetylcysteine + call transplant early King's College Criteria drives listing
Shared

Pathophysiology & classification

🧬

Mechanism — the story

The liver is the body's chemical plant, filter, and factory all at once: it synthesizes clotting factors and albumin, clears ammonia through the urea cycle, keeps glucose up and lactate down, and detoxifies drugs. In acute liver failure a sudden insult kills a critical mass of hepatocytes — by necrosis (e.g., acetaminophen, ischemia) or a mix of necrosis and apoptosis (idiosyncratic drug injury, viral, autoimmune). Cross a threshold of destroyed parenchyma and every one of those functions fails at once.

Three failures dominate the picture. (1) Synthetic failure — clotting factors (II, V, VII, IX, X) fall within hours because factor VII has a ~4–6 h half-life, so the INR climbs early and becomes the real-time readout of hepatocyte function. (2) Detoxification failure — the urea cycle can no longer convert ammonia to urea, so ammonia accumulates. Astrocytes are the only brain cells that metabolize ammonia; they convert it to glutamine, which is osmotically active, pulls water in, and swells the brain → cytotoxic cerebral edema and intracranial hypertension, the signature killer of hyperacute ALF. (3) Immune dysregulation — necrotic liver releases DAMPs driving a SIRS response, while simultaneous "immune paralysis" leaves patients profoundly prone to bacterial and fungal infection and a sepsis-like distributive (vasodilatory) shock.

The specific example worth memorizing is acetaminophen (APAP). Normally >90% is glucuronidated/sulfated safely; ~5% goes through CYP2E1 to the toxic electrophile NAPQI, which glutathione mops up. In overdose (or with alcohol/fasting inducing CYP2E1 and depleting glutathione), glutathione is exhausted, NAPQI binds mitochondrial proteins, and centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis follows. That single mechanism explains the antidote: N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and scavenges NAPQI — which is why timing is everything.

Think of the liver as a 24-hour water-treatment and power plant for a city. Knock out most of the plant at once and three crises hit together: the chemical dosing pumps stop (no clotting factors → the pipes leak = coagulopathy), the toxin scrubbers fail (ammonia floods the grid and shorts out the most sensitive district — the brain = cerebral edema), and the security system goes haywire (alarms blaring everywhere yet the gates left open = SIRS plus rampant infection). N-acetylcysteine is the emergency delivery of scrubber reagent; a transplant is building a new plant before the city goes dark.

Mechanism cascade — hepatocyte necrosis branches into synthetic, metabolic and immune failure. Green boxes show where each therapy interrupts the chain (NAC → the insult; CRRT/osmotherapy → cerebral edema; transplant → multi-organ failure).
Acetaminophen toxicity — confluent zone 3 (centrilobular) coagulative necrosis, the histologic signature of APAP-ALF (perivenular hepatocytes have the highest CYP2E1).
Dr. Linda Ferrell, UCSF Department of Pathology. · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
APAP metabolism — the minor CYP2E1 route makes toxic NAPQI; glutathione detoxifies it until overdose exhausts the supply. NAC resupplies glutathione.
Fvasconcellos · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
Every therapy in this guide maps to one arrow in the cascade. N-acetylcysteine resupplies glutathione and scavenges NAPQI at the insult step. Lactulose/rifaximin and CRRT lower ammonia; hypertonic saline/mannitol pull water back out of astrocytes at the cerebral-edema step. Nucleos(t)ide analogues, acyclovir, silibinin, steroids, or delivery each shut off a specific etiology. Norepinephrine ± vasopressin and hydrocortisone defend the arterial circulation during distributive shock. And liver transplantation replaces the whole failed plant when King's College Criteria say native recovery is unlikely.
📖

Definition, timing & encephalopathy grade

Definition (ACG 2023 / EASL 2017): evidence of coagulopathy — INR ≥ 1.5 — and any degree of hepatic encephalopathy, in a patient without pre-existing cirrhosis and with an illness of < 26 weeks. (Wilson disease, vertically-acquired HBV, and autoimmune hepatitis are still counted as ALF even if cirrhosis is discovered, provided the illness is <26 weeks.) Coagulopathy without encephalopathy is acute liver injury — watch it like a hawk; it can tip into ALF.

Don't confuse the threeALF = acute, no cirrhosis. Acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) = acute decompensation on cirrhosis with organ failure. Decompensated cirrhosis = chronic disease with ascites/varices/HE. They look alike at the bedside but the prognosis, the transplant pathway, and even whether you give lactulose all differ.

O'Grady classification — interval from jaundice to encephalopathy

SubtypeJaundice → HE intervalTypical causesCerebral edema risk / prognosis
Hyperacute< 7 daysAcetaminophen, ischemia (shock liver), HAV/HEVHighest edema risk — yet paradoxically the best spontaneous survival (esp. APAP).
Acute7–21 days (8–28 d)Non-A/non-B hepatitis, idiosyncratic DILI, HBVIntermediate edema risk; intermediate survival.
Subacute> 21 days – 26 weeks (4–26 wk)Idiosyncratic DILI, autoimmune, indeterminateLowest edema risk but worst spontaneous survival — smaller livers, silent portal hypertension; list early.

The older French (Bernuau) terms map roughly on: fulminant = HE within 2 weeks of jaundice, subfulminant = 2–12 weeks.

West Haven grading of hepatic encephalopathy

GradeMental statusNeuro signsWhat it means for you
IMild confusion, euphoria/anxiety, short attention span, altered sleepMild asterixis / tremorSubtle — trend closely; still floor-manageable.
IILethargy, disorientation to time, personality change, inappropriate behaviorObvious asterixis, slurred speechEscalation zone — arrange ICU; grade II→III can be fast.
IIISomnolent but rousable, gross disorientation, confusionRigidity, clonus, hyperreflexiaICU + intubate for airway protection; cerebral-edema precautions.
IVComa, unresponsive to painDecerebrate posturing, absent oculocephalic reflexImpending/active herniation — maximal ICP therapy.
Grade of encephalopathy is the single best bedside prognostic sign in ALF — spontaneous survival falls sharply from grade I–II to grade III–IV, and grade III/IV is a component of King's College Criteria. Serial neuro exams are a vital sign here.

Etiologies — and the test that nails each

🔎

Causes by frequency (US/Western) & the targeted work-up

Etiology drives everything — the antidote, the prognosis, and the transplant threshold. Send the whole panel on day 1; you cannot tell APAP from HSV from Wilson by looking. Frequencies are approximate US/Western figures (US ALF Study Group registry).

Cause~FrequencyClueTest to send & why
Acetaminophen~45%AST/ALT often >3500, low bilirubin early, staggered or single overdose; may be unintentionalAPAP level (4 h post-ingestion for the nomogram; send regardless of history). Very high aminotransferases + modest bilirubin = APAP or ischemia.
Idiosyncratic DILI (antibiotics, anti-TB, herbals, kratom)~11%New drug/supplement in prior 6 months; often subacuteMeticulous medication + herbal/supplement history (LiverTox); it is a diagnosis of exclusion.
Indeterminate~11%No cause found after full work-upConsider occult APAP adducts, HSV, unrecognized Wilson; worse prognosis.
Viral hepatitis (A, B, E; HSV/VZV; CMV)~12%Prodrome, exposure, immunosuppression/pregnancy (HEV, HSV)HAV IgM, HBsAg + anti-HBc IgM (± HBV DNA), HEV IgM, HSV PCR (treat empirically if suspected — HSV-ALF is lethal & treatable).
Autoimmune hepatitis~7%Female, other autoimmune disease, high globulinsANA, anti-smooth-muscle Ab, IgG level; liver biopsy (transjugular) if needed.
Ischemic (shock liver)~5%Preceding hypotension/cardiac arrest; AST/ALT in the thousands then fast fall; high LDHEcho/history; treat the hemodynamic cause — supportive, usually recovers.
Wilson disease<5%Young; Coombs-negative hemolysis; low alk phos, high bilirubin; alk phos:bilirubin <4Ceruloplasmin, serum/urine copper, slit-lamp for KF rings. Wilson-ALF = transplant (medical therapy won't rescue).
Pregnancy (AFLP / HELLP)<5%3rd trimester; AFLP with hypoglycemia; HELLP with hemolysis/low plateletsPregnancy test in every woman of child-bearing age; the treatment is prompt delivery.
Amanita / toxins, Budd-Chiari, malignant infiltration, heat stroke<5%Mushroom foraging + severe GI illness; RUQ pain + ascites (Budd-Chiari)History; RUQ Doppler US (hepatic-vein thrombosis); silibinin/penicillin G for Amanita.
Amanita phalloides (death cap) — amatoxin inhibits RNA polymerase II → hepatocyte death. Treat with silibinin, high-dose penicillin G, and NAC.

Presentation & findings — and why

🩺

Symptoms & signs — frequency and the mechanism behind each

Early ALF can be deceptively bland — especially APAP, where the first day may be only nausea. The findings below track the three failures: encephalopathy/edema (ammonia), bleeding (synthetic failure), and hemodynamic/metabolic collapse (detox + immune failure).

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Jaundice / scleral icterus~80%Failed hepatocyte conjugation + excretion of bilirubin. May lag in hyperacute APAP — a deeply encephalopathic patient can be barely icteric.
Nausea / vomiting / malaise / anorexia~75%Non-specific prodrome of hepatocellular injury and circulating toxins/cytokines; often the only early APAP symptom.
Hepatic encephalopathy (any grade)100% (by definition)Hyperammonemia → astrocyte glutamine → cerebral edema; required for the diagnosis. Ranges from subtle inattention to coma.
Coagulopathy / easy bruising / bleeding~60–70%Loss of hepatic synthesis of factors II, V, VII, IX, X. INR rises early (factor VII half-life ~4–6 h). Clinically significant spontaneous bleeding is actually uncommon (rebalanced hemostasis).
RUQ pain / tender hepatomegaly~40%Capsular stretch from acute swelling/necrosis or congestion (Budd–Chiari). A shrinking liver span is an ominous sign of massive necrosis.
Asterixis~40–50%Impaired inhibitory input from the ammonia-loaded brain → loss of postural tone (negative myoclonus). A grade I–II HE sign.
Hypotension / warm shock~20–35%SIRS-driven arterial vasodilation (↓SVR) mimicking sepsis; ↑cardiac output, low SVR — distributive physiology.
Hypoglycemia symptoms (sweating, confusion)~20–40%Loss of hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis + failure to clear insulin. Easily mistaken for worsening HE — check a glucose on every AMS.
Fetor hepaticus<15%Volatile sulfur compounds (mercaptans) exhaled when the liver can't clear them — a sweet, musty breath.
Fever / signs of sepsisVariableImmune paralysis → bacterial/fungal infection; may be blunted, so a rising pressor requirement or worsening HE can be the only clue.
Scleral icterus — visible once bilirubin exceeds ~2–3 mg/dL; the sclera shows it first because of its elastin/bilirubin affinity.
Sheila J. Toro · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Normal hepatic lobular architecture (zones 1–3). Zone 3 (perivenular) is most vulnerable to APAP and ischemia — the highest-CYP2E1, lowest-oxygen zone.

🖥️

Imaging & where it fits

StudyWhen to orderWhat it tells you
RUQ ultrasound with DopplerDay 1, everyoneExcludes cirrhosis/nodularity, checks patency of hepatic veins/portal vein (Budd–Chiari), assesses for biliary obstruction, ascites, and liver size/echotexture. First-line, no contrast, no nephrotoxicity.
CT abdomen (± contrast)If US inconclusiveBetter for vascular thrombosis, malignant infiltration, or heterogeneous necrosis; weigh contrast against frequent AKI.
Non-contrast head CTGrade III–IV HE or sudden declineLooks for cerebral edema (effaced sulci, loss of gray–white differentiation) and excludes hemorrhage before/while managing ICP. Insensitive early — a normal CT does not exclude edema.
Transthoracic echoShock / ischemic patternIdentifies the low-output state behind ischemic hepatitis and guides hemodynamic support.
Transjugular liver biopsySelected (dx unclear)Transjugular route avoids the coagulopathy; used when autoimmune, infiltration, or HSV is suspected and would change management.
Non-contrast head CT — in grade III–IV HE, look for effaced sulci and loss of gray–white differentiation (cerebral edema). Rules out hemorrhage before osmotherapy/ICP monitoring.
Goleisureintl · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Imaging supports but never makes the ALF diagnosis — that's the labs (INR + bilirubin) plus the neuro exam (HE). Use US to find the cause and head CT to manage the brain.
🧪

Reading the labs — what each value is telling you

LabWhat it means & why it moves
INR / PTThe real-time synthetic-function meter. Rises within hours because factor VII has the shortest half-life. It is a prognostic marker and a King's College criterion — so do not "correct" it prophylactically with FFP: that erases your best trend and doesn't fix the balanced coagulopathy. A rising INR despite therapy signals ongoing necrosis.
AST / ALTMarks hepatocyte injury. >3,500 (often >5,000) points to APAP, ischemia, or HSV. A falling transaminase level is ambiguous — it can mean recovery or that there are simply few hepatocytes left to lyse (read it alongside INR/bilirubin, which tell you function).
BilirubinReflects excretory failure; climbs later and higher in subacute disease. A very high bilirubin with a low alk phos in a young patient (ratio <4) flags Wilson. It's a King's College criterion in non-APAP ALF.
Ammonia (arterial)Drives encephalopathy. An arterial ammonia >150–200 µmol/L predicts intracranial hypertension and herniation risk. Draw it arterial, on ice, run quickly — tourniquet time, hemolysis and delay falsely raise venous values. Trend it, but treat the patient, not the number.
GlucoseHypoglycemia from failed gluconeogenesis/glycogenolysis is common and dangerous — it masquerades as worsening HE. Check often; many patients need a continuous D10 infusion.
Lactate / pHThe liver clears lactate; a high lactate reflects both impaired clearance and tissue hypoperfusion. Arterial pH <7.30 after resuscitation is a stand-alone King's College criterion in APAP-ALF, and early lactate refines it.
CreatinineAKI is common (hepatorenal physiology, ATN, direct APAP nephrotoxicity) and independently worsens prognosis — it's a King's College criterion in APAP-ALF and part of MELD.
PhosphateA rising phosphate suggests failed regeneration (poor prognosis); a falling phosphate can accompany hepatic regeneration (consumed by dividing cells) — but also drives weakness, so replete it.
Factor VMade only by the liver and not vitamin-K dependent — used in the French/Clichy criteria; a very low factor V (<20–30%) marks severe synthetic failure.
Coagulation cascade — the liver makes nearly every factor here and the anticoagulants (protein C/S, antithrombin), so ALF produces a rebalanced, not simply "anticoagulated," state.

Prognosis, King's College Criteria & the transplant decision

🗺️

The whole algorithm on one page

Everything in this guide funnels into one branching question — can this liver recover, or does the patient need a graft to live? The prognostic scores exist to answer it early enough to act.

ALF management algorithm — from the defining criteria through NAC and etiology-specific therapy to the King's College branch point (transplant vs. supportive ICU care) and the cerebral-edema bundle. "Call transplant + ICU early" is the highest-yield step.
🧮

King's College Criteria — interactive (the classic ALF transplant rule)

O'Grady 1989 (Gastroenterology). Pick the etiology arm, then tick what applies — the tool tells you whether the patient meets criteria for emergency transplant listing.

Etiology (pick one)
Acetaminophen APAP
Non-acetaminophen non-APAP
Acetaminophen arm
Arterial pH < 7.30 (after resuscitation) lists
— OR all three below —
INR > 6.5 (PT > 100 s) +1
Creatinine > 3.4 mg/dL (>300 µmol/L) +1
Grade III–IV encephalopathy +1
Non-acetaminophen arm
INR > 6.5 (PT > 100 s) — alone lists
— OR any 3 of 5 below —
Age < 10 or > 40 years +1
Unfavorable etiology (indeterminate / DILI / halothane) +1
Jaundice→encephalopathy > 7 days +1
INR > 3.5 (PT > 50 s) +1
Bilirubin > 17.5 mg/dL (>300 µmol/L) +1
—
KCC is highly specific (~95–100%) but only moderately sensitive (~58–68%) — meeting it means "transplant or die," but not meeting it is falsely reassuring. Add the lactate criterion (Bernal 2002: arterial lactate > 3.5 early or > 3.0 after resuscitation in APAP-ALF) and MELD, and keep trending.
📊

Other prognostic tools & listing

ToolWhat it usesHow to use it
Clichy-VillejuifHE (confusion/coma) + factor V: <20% if age <30, or <30% if age ≥30French criterion (derived in fulminant HBV); an alternative listing trigger where factor V is measured.
MELD / MELD 3.0Bilirubin, INR, creatinine (± Na, albumin, sex)ACG 2023 endorses KCC or MELD; MELD > 25 flags high risk. MELD tends to beat KCC in non-APAP ALF. Compute on MDCalc (don't hand-reimplement the coefficients).
ALFSG Prognostic IndexComa grade + bilirubin + INR + phosphate + M30 (CK-18)Outperformed KCC (AUROC 0.82 vs 0.65) but M30 isn't routine — a research/triage tool.
UNOS Status 1AFulminant ALF, HE onset <8 wk, life expectancy <7 d, ICU-level illness with ≥1 of: vent, RRT, or INR > 2.0 (or fulminant Wilson)The listing status for ALF — the highest transplant priority.

Transplant-free survival is etiology-driven: acetaminophen and ischemic/pregnancy causes do relatively well (~60–65%), while indeterminate, idiosyncratic DILI, autoimmune, Budd–Chiari, and Wilson do poorly (~25% or less; fulminant Wilson ≈ 0% without a graft).

Comorbidity interactions & drugs to avoid

🔗

How common comorbidities change the course — and the management

ComorbidityHow it changes the diseaseHow it changes management
Chronic alcohol use / malnutrition / fastingInduces CYP2E1 and depletes glutathione → lowers the APAP toxicity threshold (toxicity at "therapeutic" doses — the classic "therapeutic misadventure").Give NAC at a low threshold even without a large ingestion; add thiamine and watch for Wernicke/withdrawal.
Pregnancy (3rd trimester)Points to AFLP / HELLP, and to severe HEV and HSV hepatitis.Prompt delivery for AFLP/HELLP; empiric acyclovir; co-manage with OB and transplant.
CKD / AKIAKI is common (hepatorenal-type, ATN, direct APAP nephrotoxicity) and is a King's College / MELD variable that worsens prognosis.Renally dose-adjust drugs; avoid nephrotoxins; CRRT does double duty (renal + ammonia).
Chronic HBVReactivation (after chemo/immunosuppression) can precipitate ALF — an "ALF despite underlying disease" scenario.Start entecavir/tenofovir; screen before immunosuppression (USPSTF).
Diabetes / obesity / NAFLDReduced hepatic reserve; obesity complicates weight-based dosing.Cap NAC dosing weight at 100 kg; hold metformin/SGLT2i (lactic acidosis / euglycemic DKA risk).
Heart failure / shock statesDrives ischemic hepatitis ("shock liver") — AST/ALT in the thousands with early LDH rise.Treat the hemodynamic cause; NAC is not specifically indicated for pure ischemic hepatitis; it usually recovers with perfusion.
Drugs to avoid / use with caution in ALF
  • Prophylactic FFP/PCC "to fix the INR" — masks the best prognostic trend, causes volume overload/TRALI/↑ICP, doesn't prevent meaningful bleeding. Transfuse only for active bleeding or procedures.
  • NSAIDs & aminoglycosides & excess IV contrast — nephrotoxic; protect the kidney (a KCC/MELD variable).
  • Intermittent hemodialysis for ammonia — osmolar shifts worsen cerebral edema; use continuous RRT.
  • Long-acting benzodiazepines / opioids — mask the neuro exam and accumulate; if sedation is needed use propofol ± dexmedetomidine.
  • More acetaminophen / other hepatotoxins — stop all non-essential and hepatotoxic drugs; scrutinize herbals/supplements.
  • Routine cirrhotic-intensity lactulose — caution in ALF (ileus/distension can jeopardize transplant); it does not replace CRRT.
  • Metformin / SGLT2 inhibitors — hold in the acutely ill ALF patient (lactic acidosis / euglycemic DKA).
🩺 Clinic / early ED — recognize, start the antidote, and transfer
FramingALF is never a "manage-in-clinic" disease. The outpatient/urgent-care/early-ED job is a five-minute one: recognize it, draw the panel, give N-acetylcysteine, protect glucose, and move the patient to a hospital with a transplant service before the brain and hemodynamics fail. Everything here is a bridge.
Assess

When to suspect

🔍

Who walks in with early ALF

  • The acetaminophen story — an intentional overdose, or the far sneakier unintentional "therapeutic misadventure": someone taking a combination cold product + a separate APAP + an opioid–APAP tablet, often fasting or drinking, now nauseated with rising transaminases. Suspect it even without a clear history.
  • New jaundice + confusion — the combination of scleral icterus and any altered mentation (even mild inattention or reversed sleep) in a previously well person is ALF until proven otherwise.
  • A "viral" illness that won't quit — prodrome, then deepening malaise, dark urine, bruising.
  • At-risk hosts — chronic alcohol use, malnutrition/fasting, recent new medication or herbal/supplement, pregnancy (3rd trimester), immunosuppression (HSV), mushroom foraging.
Jaundice + confusion, asterixis, spontaneous bruising/bleeding, hypoglycemia, or a known large APAP ingestion = call EMS for transfer, don't send home to "recheck labs next week."
Workup

What to order & when

🧪

The day-1 panel — send it all at once

Start the antidote & stabilize

💊

First-line → escalation — the outpatient/ED bridge

1
N-acetylcysteine — give early, ask questions later
Antidote for APAP and beneficial in early non-APAP ALF.
▾
NAC resupplies glutathione so it can neutralize NAPQI, and independently improves microcirculatory oxygen delivery. In the US ALF Study Group RCT (Lee 2009) it improved transplant-free survival in early-grade (I–II) HE even in non-acetaminophen ALF — so start it while the work-up is pending.
AgentStart (loading)Then (titration / maintenance)Why it worksIf reaction / alt
N-acetylcysteine (IV, 21-h protocol)150 mg/kg in D5W over 60 min50 mg/kg over 4 h → 100 mg/kg over 16 h; continue at 6.25 mg/kg/h in ALF until INR < 1.5, transplant, or recovery. Dose on actual weight, cap at 100 kg.Glutathione precursor scavenges NAPQI; also antioxidant + vasodilatory O₂ delivery.Anaphylactoid reaction (flushing/wheeze) → pause, antihistamine, restart slower. True allergy is rare; oral NAC 140 mg/kg then 70 mg/kg q4h × 17 is an alternative.
N-acetylcysteine (2-bag, increasingly used)200 mg/kg over 4 h100 mg/kg over 16 h (same 300 mg/kg total, fewer anaphylactoid reactions vs the 3-bag).Same mechanism; simpler, better tolerated.Use institutional protocol/toxicology.
Activated charcoal1 g/kg PO/NG onceOnly if within ~1–2 h of ingestion and airway protected.Adsorbs unabsorbed APAP in the gut.Skip if aspiration risk / late presentation.
If you don't know the ingestion time or it's a staggered/repeated-supratherapeutic pattern, treat — the nomogram only applies to a single acute ingestion with a known time. When in doubt, NAC is safe; not giving it is not.
2
Protect the brain & the sugar — simple bedside moves
Glucose, avoid sedatives, treat the treatable cause.
▾
  • Dextrose — check glucose now and hourly; start D10 infusion if < 70 mg/dL (hypoglycemia mimics and worsens HE).
  • Avoid sedatives / benzodiazepines / opioids — they cloud the neuro exam you're relying on and can precipitate deeper HE; avoid additional hepatotoxins and nephrotoxins (NSAIDs).
  • Etiology-specific antidote if obvious — empiric acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h if HSV possible; penicillin G + silibinin for Amanita; nucleos(t)ide analogue for HBV; expedite delivery in AFLP/HELLP.
3
Transfer to a transplant center — now, not after labs return
Time is brain and time is a graft.
▾

Any confirmed ALF (INR ≥ 1.5 + HE) or high-risk acute liver injury (e.g., APAP with rising INR) warrants a call to the nearest transplant hepatology service and inter-facility transfer, ideally before grade III–IV HE develops (safer to transport, and listing takes time). Send copies of all labs and the ingestion history with the patient.

Monitor

The acute-liver-injury not-yet-ALF patient

📈

What to recheck, and when

If the patient has coagulopathy but no encephalopathy (acute liver injury), they are one step from ALF. In a monitored setting recheck INR, transaminases, bilirubin, creatinine and glucose every 6–12 h, and perform serial neuro exams for the first sign of HE. A rising INR, a falling glucose, or new confusion means the trajectory is ALF — escalate. Do not discharge an acute-liver-injury patient with a rising INR.

Repeat the APAP level and LFTs in staggered/unknown-timing ingestions; the first level can be low while injury is still evolving.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B & prevention

🛡️

Grade A & B recommendations that touch ALF

GradeRecommendationPopulation / relevance to ALF
BScreen for hepatitis B virus infectionAdults/adolescents at increased risk — prevents HBV-ALF & identifies reactivation risk before immunosuppression.
BScreen for hepatitis C virus infectionAll adults 18–79 — chronic HCV context; treat before it complicates.
BUnhealthy alcohol use screening & brief counselingAdults ≥ 18 — alcohol induces CYP2E1/depletes glutathione, magnifying APAP toxicity.
BScreen for illicit/prescription drug useAdults — identifies overdose & supplement/herbal DILI risk.

Vaccinate & counsel: hepatitis A and hepatitis B vaccination (ACIP now recommends universal HepB for adults 19–59); counsel every patient that the maximum acetaminophen dose is ≤ 4 g/day (≤ 2–3 g/day with liver disease, chronic alcohol, or malnutrition), and that it hides in combination cold and opioid products. Educate foragers about Amanita.

Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Red flags → ED & transplant center

Transfer immediately for any of: INR ≥ 1.5 with encephalopathy (= ALF); INR rising despite NAC; grade II+ HE, agitation or somnolence; hypoglycemia; arterial pH < 7.30 or lactate > 3.5; creatinine rising; a large or unknown-timing APAP ingestion.
Grade III–IV HE, seizure, or signs of raised ICP (hypertension + bradycardia, unequal pupils, posturing) = airway + ICU-level transport with the head of the bed at 30°. This is a neurologic emergency, not just a liver problem.
🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient management
FramingConfirmed ALF is never really a floor disease — the "wards" here means a monitored/step-down bed at a transplant center while you stabilize, hunt the cause, run the antidote, and watch the neuro exam like a hawk. The floor job is to catch the tip into grade II+ HE, shock, or rising ammonia before it becomes a crash. If your hospital has no transplant service, the admission task is simultaneous stabilization and transfer.
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & where they belong

  • Admit every ALF (INR ≥ 1.5 + any HE, no cirrhosis, <26 wk) — no exceptions, and to a transplant center.
  • Admit high-risk acute liver injury (INR rising, bilirubin climbing, large/uncertain APAP ingestion) even without HE — it is one neuro check from ALF.
  • Level of care: grade 0–I HE with stable/improving INR and immediate escalation capability can start in a monitored step-down bed; grade II that is progressing, any hemodynamic instability, or airway concern → ICU (see Escalate).
The single most important admission order is a phone call: contact transplant hepatology in the first hours — before grade III–IV HE — because listing takes time and a grade IV patient is dangerous to transport. Send the ingestion history and all labs with any transfer.
Orders

Admission order set

🧪

Labs, imaging, monitoring, consults

Treat

Acute management

💊

Stepwise inpatient therapy — antidote, cause, support

1
Continue / start N-acetylcysteine
Don't stop at a fixed 21 h if INR/enzymes still worsening.
▾

Run the IV protocol (150 mg/kg over 60 min → 50 mg/kg over 4 h → 100 mg/kg over 16 h; dose on actual weight capped at 100 kg), then continue at 6.25 mg/kg/h until INR < 1.5, transplant, or clear recovery (2023 US–Canada consensus: continue to stopping criteria, don't stop by the clock). NAC also benefits early-grade non-APAP ALF (Lee 2009).

2
Etiology-specific therapy — the whole point of the day-1 panel
Each cause has its own antidote; give it early.
▾
CauseStartTitration / targetWhy it worksIf allergic / alt
HSV / VZV hepatitisAcyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8hContinue 7–14 d; keep well hydrated (crystalluria/AKI). Give empirically while PCR pends.Halts viral hepatocyte lysis; HSV-ALF is often anicteric and lethal if missed.Foscarnet if acyclovir-resistant HSV/renal-dose concerns.
Hepatitis B (acute or reactivation)Entecavir 0.5 mg PO daily or tenofovir DF 300 mg PO dailyRenal-dose adjust; continue indefinitely; check HDV co-infection.Suppresses HBV replication; essential before/with immunosuppression.Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) if renal/bone concern.
Amanita (amatoxin)Silibinin 5 mg/kg IV loadthen 20 mg/kg/day continuous infusion; + penicillin G ~1,000,000 units/kg/day (ACG: up to 1.5 million/kg/day on days 2–3) + NAC + multi-dose charcoal.Blocks amatoxin hepatocyte uptake; interrupts enterohepatic recycling.If no silibinin: high-dose penicillin G + NAC + MDAC.
Autoimmune hepatitisMethylprednisolone ~60 mg/day IV (weak evidence)Reassess in days; do not delay transplant listing for a steroid trial.Suppresses the autoimmune attack — but ALFSG data show no survival benefit and harm in high-MELD.Skip steroids and prioritize transplant if high MELD / infected.
AFLP / HELLPPrompt deliverySupportive care post-delivery; recovery is the norm.Removes the placental driver of the injury.—
Wilson (fulminant)List for transplant (Status 1A)Bridge with plasma exchange / albumin dialysis / CRRT to lower copper.Medical chelation cannot rescue fulminant Wilson (spontaneous survival ≈ 0%).—
3
Supportive bundle — protect brain, sugar, clotting, gut
The daily physiology that keeps them alive to transplant or recovery.
▾
  • Glucose: continuous D10W (escalate to D20 via central line) to keep glucose ~140–180 mg/dL; never let it fall.
  • Electrolytes: aggressively replete K, Mg, phosphate (repletion supports regeneration and prevents arrhythmia/weakness).
  • Coagulopathy — do NOT prophylactically transfuse. Give vitamin K 10 mg IV once. FFP/PCC/cryoprecipitate/platelets only for active bleeding or before a procedure (cryo if fibrinogen < ~100–120 mg/dL). Correcting the INR erases your best prognostic trend.
  • Stress-ulcer prophylaxis: pantoprazole 40 mg IV daily.
  • Nutrition: feed early enterally; do NOT protein-restrict — target ~1–1.5 g/kg/day protein.
  • Infection surveillance: low threshold for cultures and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics ± antifungals — occult infection precipitates HE and can de-list a patient.
  • HE/ammonia: lactulose is used cautiously in ALF (ileus/distension can jeopardize transplant, unproven benefit) — the real ammonia tool is CRRT (ICU). Avoid sedatives that mask the exam.
Stop every non-essential and potentially hepatotoxic/nephrotoxic drug: no more APAP, no NSAIDs, no aminoglycosides, minimize IV contrast, hold metformin/SGLT2i. Scrutinize the home/herbal/supplement list line by line.
Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend, and how to read the trend

The ALF flowsheet: INR, arterial ammonia, lactate, pH, creatinine, glucose (q1–2h), phosphate, bilirubin, and the West Haven grade — the same variables that feed King's College and MELD.

TrendInterpretationAction
Falling phosphate + stabilizing INR + clearing sensoriumHepatic regeneration — the liver is coming back.Continue support; keep watching.
Rising INR / lactate / creatinine or deepening HEDeteriorating — trajectory toward death without transplant.Confirm transplant listing; escalate to ICU; recheck King's College.
Ammonia climbing toward 150–200 µmol/LRising intracranial-hypertension risk.ICU; osmotherapy planning + early CRRT.
A falling transaminase is ambiguous — it can mean recovery or that there is little liver left to lyse. Always read AST/ALT next to INR and bilirubin (function), not alone.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Concrete escalation triggers

Transfer to ICU for any of:
  • HE grade ≥ II and progressing, agitation, or somnolence (grade III–IV → intubate for airway).
  • Arterial ammonia > 150–200 µmol/L or rising despite therapy (cerebral-edema/CRRT territory).
  • Hemodynamic instability — MAP < 65 mmHg or a new pressor requirement; lactate > 3–3.5 mmol/L.
  • Hypoglycemia refractory to D10, needing central D20/D50.
  • AKI (rising creatinine / oliguria) needing CRRT, or acidosis pH < 7.30.
  • Any patient meeting King's College Criteria or actively listed for transplant.
Cushing reflex (hypertension + bradycardia), unequal/sluggish pupils, or posturing = impending herniation. Head of bed 30°, hyperosmolar therapy, call ICU/neurosurgery and transplant simultaneously.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: HE fully resolved and mentation at baseline; INR trending to normal without transfusion; tolerating oral intake with stable glucose; the cause addressed (antiviral started, offending drug stopped, delivered, transplanted); and — for any intentional overdose — a completed psychiatric/safety evaluation before discharge (non-negotiable). Post-transplant patients leave on immunosuppression with transplant-center follow-up.

Home

Recovered ALI/ALF, INR normalized, baseline mentation, reliable support; APAP-overdose survivors after psych clearance + poison-center/hepatology follow-up.

Home health

Home + skilled nursing/labs/therapy visits — e.g., new anticoagulation for Budd–Chiari or wound care.

SNF

Deconditioned but medically stable; needs 24-h skilled nursing, <3 h therapy/day.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Post-ICU/post-transplant deconditioning; can tolerate ≥3 h therapy/day across ≥2 disciplines.

LTAC

Prolonged complex needs — ventilator weaning, extended CRRT, complex post-transplant course.

Hospice / palliative

Meets King's College but not a transplant candidate (declined, contraindicated, or malignant infiltration) — comfort-focused, goals-of-care.
🫀 ICU — critical care & organ support
FramingThe ICU job in ALF is to buy time — keep the brain from herniating and the circulation from collapsing — until the liver regenerates or a graft arrives. Two things kill: cerebral edema/intracranial hypertension and sepsis/multi-organ failure. Every intervention below defends one of those fronts while the transplant clock runs.
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When it belongs in the unit — and the edema risk that drives it

ICU for HE grade III–IV, cerebral edema/intracranial hypertension, distributive shock, respiratory failure, need for CRRT, or refractory metabolic derangement. The reason grade of HE is the trigger: cerebral-edema risk climbs steeply with it.

HE gradeCerebral-edema riskICU posture
I–IILowMonitored bed; frequent neuro checks; ICU if progressing.
III~25–35%ICU + intubate for airway; start edema precautions.
IV~65–75%Maximal ICP therapy; herniation is a leading mode of death.
Targets once here: MAP ≥ 65 mmHg, CPP ≥ 50–60 mmHg (= MAP − ICP), ICP < 20–25 mmHg, serum Na 145–155, glucose 140–180, arterial ammonia falling toward < 60, and strict normothermia.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, neuro monitoring, targets

  • Arterial line — continuous MAP for CPP, and frequent ABG / lactate / arterial ammonia sampling.
  • Central venous access — vasopressors, concentrated dextrose (D20/D50), and CRRT circuit.
  • Neuro monitoring — hourly exam + pupils/pupillometry; non-invasive surrogates (transcranial Doppler, optic-nerve-sheath diameter, jugular venous O₂ saturation). Invasive ICP monitoring is controversial — ACG 2023 says consider only at centers with expertise, in highly selected listed patients, because a bolt in a coagulopathic brain risks hemorrhage.
  • Trend the ALF flowsheet hourly-to-q4h: ammonia, lactate, pH, glucose (q1–2h), Na (for the osmotherapy target), INR, creatinine, phosphate.
Support

Pressors & inotropes

💉

Distributive shock — which drip, why, and the dose

ALF shock is vasodilatory/distributive (SIRS + failed clearance of vasoactive substances) — physiology like sepsis: low SVR, high output. Resuscitate with balanced crystalloid (avoid hypotonic fluids that worsen edema), then layer pressors to a MAP ≥ 65 (and CPP ≥ 50–60 if ICP known).

AgentReceptors / mechanismDose (start → titrate)Hemodynamic effectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα₁ ≫ β₁ vasoconstriction0.05 mcg/kg/min → up to ~3 mcg/kg/min, titrate to MAP ≥ 65↑SVR, mild ↑COFirst-line ALF distributive shock
VasopressinV₁ receptor (catecholamine-sparing)0.03 units/min fixed add-on (not titrated)↑SVRSecond agent to spare catecholamines; caution in severe intracranial hypertension (theoretical cerebral vasodilation)
HydrocortisoneRestores vascular catecholamine responsiveness; treats relative adrenal insufficiency ("hepatoadrenal")200–300 mg/day (50 mg IV q6h or infusion)↓pressor requirementVasopressor-refractory shock
Epinephrineβ₁/β₂ + α₁0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑CO, ↑SVR (↑lactate)Add-on if refractory; note it raises lactate (a prognostic marker here)
Match receptor to goal: the problem is low SVR, so lead with the α₁-dominant agent (norepinephrine); add V₁ (vasopressin) to spare catecholamines; and add hydrocortisone when the vessels stop responding — the classic signature of relative adrenal insufficiency in liver failure.
Airway

Respiratory support & vent

🌬️

Intubate to protect the brain — settings that don't raise ICP

Intubate at HE grade III–IV for airway protection (lost reflexes, aspiration risk) — NIV has little role in the encephalopathic ALF patient. Sedate with propofol (short-acting and lowers cerebral metabolic rate) ± dexmedetomidine; avoid long-acting benzodiazepines/opioids that mask the neuro exam and accumulate.

Mode
AC/VC

The brain, not the lung, dictates the vent here: keep PaCO₂ low-normal, PEEP modest, and reserve deliberate hyperventilation for an acute ICP/herniation crisis (rebound follows sustained use).
Neuro

Cerebral edema / ICP bundle

🧠

The intracranial-hypertension protocol — exact doses

General measures first: head of bed 30°, head/neck midline (no jugular compression), minimize stimulation/suctioning, aggressive normothermia, treat seizures, avoid hyponatremia and hypercarbia.

TherapyStartTitration / targetWhy it worksCaution / alt
Hypertonic saline (first-line)3% infusion (or 23.4% bolus for surges)Titrate to serum Na 145–155 mmol/L (prophylactic mild hypernatremia lowers ICP surges — Murphy 2004)Osmotic gradient pulls water out of swollen astrocytes.Watch for volume overload; central line for concentrated saline.
Mannitol (osmotic bolus)0.5–1 g/kg IV (≈ 50–100 g)May repeat if serum osmolality < 320 mOsm/L; MAHAL RCT: comparable to hypertonic salineOsmotic diuresis + rheologic effect drops ICP.Caution in AKI (osmotic load, volume); needs urine output.
HyperventilationPaCO₂ 25–35 mmHgTemporizing bridge only for acute herniationCerebral vasoconstriction rapidly lowers ICP.Rebound with sustained use — not a maintenance strategy.
CRRT (ammonia control)Continuous modality — start earlyFor ammonia > 150–200 or HE ≥ II; target ammonia < 60Directly removes the osmotic driver (ammonia→glutamine).Never intermittent HD — osmolar shifts worsen edema.
Therapeutic hypothermia33–35 °C (salvage only)Bridge for refractory ICH; not routineLowers cerebral metabolism/ammonia production.Bernal 2016 RCT: no ICP benefit vs normothermia — reserve as rescue.
Grade III–IV HE — get a non-contrast head CT to exclude hemorrhage and look for effaced sulci / lost gray–white differentiation. A normal early CT does not exclude edema; treat by the ammonia, exam, and (if placed) ICP.

Rescue

Advanced / extracorporeal support & transplant

⚙️

CRRT, plasma exchange, and the definitive fix

1
CRRT — the ammonia workhorse
Continuous, not intermittent. Start early.
▾

ACG 2023 endorses CRRT for significant HE + hyperammonemia even without traditional renal indications. Practically: arterial ammonia > 150–200 µmol/L or rising, or HE grade ≥ II. Use a continuous modality (CVVH/CVVHD/CVVHDF) — intermittent HD's rapid osmolar/urea shifts worsen cerebral edema. Higher effluent dose and earlier/longer therapy clear more ammonia (target < 60 µmol/L); follow nephrology/unit protocol for the exact dose.

2
High-volume plasma exchange (HVP)
The one extracorporeal therapy with an RCT survival benefit.
▾

Larsen 2016 (J Hepatol, n=182): HVP — exchange of 8–12–15% of ideal body weight with FFP over 3 days — plus standard care improved transplant-free survival (~59% vs 48%), with benefit mainly in patients not transplanted. It works by clearing DAMPs and dampening the inflammatory cascade. Standard-volume PLEX (Maiwall 2021) also helped. Consider in patients not immediately transplantable or as a bridge.

3
Albumin dialysis (MARS / Prometheus)
Bridge only.
▾

Improves biochemistry and HE transiently but no clear survival benefit in RCTs (FULMAR/MARS). Use as a temporizing bridge to transplant or recovery, not as definitive therapy.

4
Liver transplantation — the definitive therapy
~25–30% of ALF patients are transplanted.
▾

When the native liver won't recover, transplant is the only cure. List as UNOS Status 1A (highest urgency) — fulminant ALF with life expectancy < 7 days, HE onset within 8 weeks, no pre-existing liver disease, ICU-level illness with ≥ 1 of ventilator dependence, renal replacement therapy, or INR > 2.0 (fulminant Wilson also qualifies). King's College Criteria and MELD drive listing and prognosis (see the shared Prognosis section). Contraindications: uncontrolled sepsis, irreversible brain injury/fixed pupils with sustained high ICP, malignant infiltration, and severe cardiopulmonary disease.

Orthotopic liver transplant — definitive therapy for ALF meeting transplant criteria. Auxiliary (partial) transplant is an option in select patients whose native liver may regenerate.
Aphelpsmd · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Step down when all are true: HE improving to grade ≤ I with intact airway reflexes (successfully extubated), INR stabilizing/falling (regeneration) or successful transplant, off or weaning vasopressors, arterial ammonia and lactate normalizing, and resolving cerebral edema.
Not yet if: ammonia still > 150 µmol/L, any pressor requirement, unextubated grade III–IV HE, ongoing CRRT for ammonia, or a still-rising INR — these belong in the unit, listed and watched.

ICU disposition paths: recovery (regenerated native liver) → floor → rehab; transplanted → post-transplant floor/step-down on immunosuppression; or, if King's College is met but the patient is not a transplant candidate, transition to comfort-focused / palliative care with the family.

Educational reference for an incoming IM resident. Every dose, threshold, and criterion should be verified against the current ACG 2023 / EASL 2017 text, a maintained calculator (MDCalc/OPTN), your regional poison-control center, and institutional/transplant-center protocols before acting on any individual patient. Where a figure here disagrees with the primary guideline, the guideline governs.
